paper.title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
paper.central_claim: Voyager, an LLM-driven agent combining an automatic curriculum, an ever-growing executable skill library and an iterative prompting mechanism with execution feedback and self-verification, continually explores Minecraft and acquires reusable skills without model fine-tuning, outperforming adapted LLM-agent baselines and reusing its library in a new world.

provenance.notes: actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref not exposed to the worker in this subagent context; model_type is the configured type only.

Appendix B (setup, baselines, ablations, per-trial results, retrieval accuracy, model variation)

evidence.quote: an ever-growing skill library of executable code for storing and retrieving complex behaviors
evidence.support_explanation: Central retained component: executable-code skill library; with the curriculum and iterative prompting it forms the claimed lifelong-learning agent.

evidence.quote: Each time GPT-4 generates and verifies a new skill, we add it to the skill library, represented by a vector database.
evidence.support_explanation: Write path: verified skill appended to a vector DB (key = embedding of GPT-3.5 description, value = program).

evidence.quote: This iterative process repeats until self-verification validates the task’s completion, at which point we add this new skill to the skill library and ask the automatic curriculum for a new objective
evidence.support_explanation: Acceptance rule: the LLM self-verifier decides admission and moves the curriculum on.

evidence.quote: If the agent gets stuck after 4 rounds of code generation, then we query the curriculum for another task.
evidence.support_explanation: Failure handling: 4-round cap; unsolved task recorded as failed (Algorithm 1) but no repair of earlier skills.

evidence.quote: Instead of manually coding success checkers for each new task proposed by the automatic curriculum, we instantiate another GPT-4 agent for self-verification.
evidence.support_explanation: Admission gate is a GPT-4 critic reading agent state, not an execution-based checker.

evidence.quote: Occasionally, self-verification module may also fail, such as not recognizing spider string as a success signal of beating a spider.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors acknowledge critic false negatives; no measured critic accuracy is reported.

evidence.quote: Each program is indexed by the embedding of its description, which can be retrieved in similar situations in the future.
evidence.support_explanation: Retrieval design: embedding index over skill descriptions; top-5 skills enter the next prompt.

evidence.quote: The top-5 accuracy standing at 96.5% suggests our retrieval process is reliable
evidence.support_explanation: Only retrieval is measured directly (309 samples), not skill correctness.

evidence.quote: Previously completed and failed tasks
evidence.support_explanation: Curriculum input includes completed and failed task lists (state in prompt), so progress persists as text lists.

evidence.quote: to generate environment feedback and prompt GPT-4 to use this function as well during code generation;
evidence.support_explanation: Environment feedback depends on human-engineered bot.chat() hooks inside control-primitive APIs.

evidence.quote: Control primitive APIs implemented by us
evidence.support_explanation: Human-authored primitive API layer the generated skills call; skills compose over a fixed human-built interface.

evidence.quote: Because there is no LLM-based agents that work out of the box for Minecraft, we make our best effort to select a number of representative algorithms as baselines.
evidence.support_explanation: Baselines (ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT) are reinterpreted NLP agents with no skill library or curriculum, so comparison conflates components.

evidence.quote: discovering 63 unique items within 160 prompting iterations
evidence.support_explanation: Headline exploration result; three trials per method (App B.4.1); unique-item count aligns with the curriculum's own objective.

evidence.quote: We run three trials for each method.
evidence.support_explanation: n = 3 trials per method; Table 1 reports mean +/- SD of iterations and success fractions, no tests.

evidence.quote: we clear the agent’s inventory, reset it to a newly instantiated world, and test it with unseen tasks.
evidence.support_explanation: Held-out style test: skill library from lifelong run reused in a fresh world on 4 unseen tasks; Table 2 numbers: Voyager 19+-3, 18+-7, 21+-5, 18+-2 iterations (3/3 each) vs Voyager w/o skill library 36 (2/3), 30+-9, 27+-9, 26+-3 and AutoGPT 0/3; which lifelong run supplied the library and overlap with practised skills are not stated.

evidence.quote: This demonstrates that the skill library serves as a versatile tool that can be readily employed by other methods
evidence.support_explanation: Library transplanted into AutoGPT: 1/3, 1/3, 0/3, 2/3 successes on the 4 tasks, i.e. weak positive transfer.

evidence.quote: exhibits a tendency to plateau in the later stages.
evidence.support_explanation: Skill-library ablation in exploration is reported qualitatively (Fig 9); Table 1 shows w/o library 7+-2, 9+-4, 29+-11 iterations and 0/3 diamond vs Voyager 6+-2, 11+-2, 21+-7 and 1/3.

evidence.quote: The discovered item count drops by
evidence.support_explanation: Random-curriculum ablation: -93% items; self-verification removal -73% (Sec 3.4); numbers in prose, curves only in Fig 9.

evidence.quote: GPT-4 significantly outperforms GPT-3.5 in code generation
evidence.support_explanation: Backbone dependence: GPT-3.5 yields 5.7x fewer unique items; code quality of GPT-4 is a prerequisite.

evidence.quote: find that the performance is roughly the same
evidence.support_explanation: gpt-4-0314 vs gpt-4-0613 comparison (Fig A.4) as robustness to model version.

evidence.quote: The GPT-4 API incurs significant costs.
evidence.support_explanation: Only qualitative cost statement (15x GPT-3.5); no token/dollar accounting per method or for building the library.

evidence.quote: The automatic curriculum occasionally proposes unachievable tasks.
evidence.support_explanation: Curriculum hallucination (e.g. nonexistent copper sword) wastes iterations; admission relies on later critic/failed-task lists.

evidence.quote: Our approach bypasses the need for model parameter access and explicit gradient-based training or finetuning.
evidence.support_explanation: Non-weight claim: all learning is in prompts, task lists and the executable skill library.

evidence.quote: Hence, our self-verification is more comprehensive than self-reflection
evidence.support_explanation: Critic returns success boolean and critique; critique feeds back into code refinement.

gap.author_gap: LLM agents are not lifelong learners that progressively acquire, update, accumulate and transfer knowledge; prior LLM agents lack an automatic curriculum, an executable skill library and combined feedback.
gap.checked_gap: Partly confirmed by in-paper baselines (ReAct, Reflexion 0/3 on every tech-tree level, AutoGPT stalls before diamond), but baselines are re-interpreted NLP agents that lack the mechanisms by construction, so the residual bottleneck is shown only against weak comparators.
lineage: Code as Policies / ProgPrompt: LLM-written programs as policies, no persistent library
Reflexion / ReAct / AutoGPT: feedback or decomposition loops, no reusable executable store
Generative Agents: memory of experience, actions not executable
DECKARD / DEPS / Plan4MC: human recipe-guided subgoals or pre-defined skills (Table A.2)
Voyager: curriculum + self-written skill library + execution/critic loop with no gradient updates
closest_adjacent: Generative Agents (stores experiences as memories, non-executable actions) - not compared experimentally
Code as Policies / ProgPrompt - executable policies but no accumulation
Plan4MC / DEPS - skill-based but human-specified skills (pre-defined)
gap.residue: Missing in prior LLM agents: self-generated, executable, composable skills that persist and transfer across tasks and worlds.
gap.stakes: Without persistence, long-horizon Minecraft progress (tech tree) stalls (baselines 0/3 beyond iron).
gap.method_response: Verified skill write-back, embedding retrieval, state-conditioned curriculum, execution/critic feedback.
gap.remaining_gap: Skill correctness is judged by an LLM critic; no library maintenance (dedup, retire, conflict); GPT-4 cost; single environment family with human-built primitives.
unresolved: Nearest-neighbour originals (Code as Policies, Generative Agents, DECKARD/DEPS) are not in the pinned materials; lineage rests on Voyager Sec 5 and Table A.2.

claims.text: Voyager obtains 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distance and unlocks tech-tree levels up to 15.3x faster than ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT
claims.setting: Minecraft/MineDojo + Mineflayer, GPT-4, 160 prompting iterations, 3 trials
claims.selection_vs_test: lifelong stream; no held-out split for this claim
claims.result_denominator: 3 trials; Table 1 success fractions incl. 0/3 entries; diamond only 1/3 for Voyager
claims.counterevidence: Baselines lack curriculum/library by design; unique-item metric aligned with curriculum goal
claims.allowed_conclusion: Against these adapted baselines the full system progresses faster; no claim about stronger baselines.

claims.text: Each component (curriculum, skill library, environment feedback, execution errors, self-verification, GPT-4) matters for exploration
claims.setting: ablations over exploration, 3 trials (assumed same protocol)
claims.result_denominator: curves in Fig 9; percentages in text (random curriculum -93%, no self-verification -73%, GPT-3.5 5.7x fewer)
claims.counterevidence: Skill-library effect on tech-tree speed is small except iron/diamond; numeric ablation table absent
claims.allowed_conclusion: Curriculum, self-verification and GPT-4 clearly matter; skill library effect mostly late-stage.

claims.text: Skill library built in lifelong learning transfers to a fresh world and unseen tasks, outperforming no-library variants and baselines
claims.setting: new world, 4 tasks, 50 iteration cap, 3 trials
claims.baseline_control: Voyager w/o skill library; AutoGPT with/without library
claims.selection_vs_test: library from lifelong run vs unseen tasks in new world
claims.result_denominator: Voyager 3/3 on all four; w/o library 2/3,3/3,3/3,3/3; AutoGPT 0/3 (with library 1/3,1/3,0/3,2/3)
claims.counterevidence: library provenance and overlap with practised skills unspecified
claims.allowed_conclusion: Retained library reduces iterations (about 1.3-1.9x) on four tech-tree tasks in a new Minecraft world.

claims.text: Voyager learns lifelong without human intervention and bypasses fine-tuning
claims.counterevidence: Human-built primitive APIs, feedback hooks, prompts; library never maintained
claims.allowed_conclusion: No weight updates (supported); "lifelong" and "no human involvement" only up to 160 iterations with hand-built scaffolding.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: A skill library written by GPT-4 during a 160-iteration run speeds up four unseen Minecraft tech-tree tasks in a new world (about 1.3-1.9x fewer iterations than the same agent without the library, 3 trials), and the full system progresses faster than adapted ReAct/Reflexion/AutoGPT baselines on exploration metrics.
unresolved: No improver-level claim; library maintenance not studied.
Provenance and overlap of the library used in the zero-shot test unspecified.
Critic accuracy not measured; baseline strength limited.

G.reason: Specific gap (LLM agents without accumulating, executable, transferable knowledge) positioned against ReAct/Reflexion/AutoGPT/Generative Agents/Code-as-Policies/DECKARD-DEPS-Plan4MC with a system-level comparison table and a stated list of limits. Not 4 because the nearest executable-policy neighbours are not compared experimentally and the bottleneck is demonstrated only against adapted baselines.

M.reason: Closed mechanism from execution feedback to candidate (code), accept/reject (critic), write-back (embedding index) and later reuse (top-5 retrieval) with component ablations and a clear explanation of why programs compose. Assumes the LLM critic is a reliable verifier and that hand-built primitives expose enough feedback.

X.reason: Pseudocode, prompts, hyper-parameters (4 rounds, top-5, warm-up schedule) and retrieval measurements make the loop reconstructible; limitations are listed. Retention conditions are thin: no dedup, versioning, retirement or conflict handling, and abstraction validity is not checked beyond the originating task.

E.measurement.reason: Unique items, tech-tree milestones and task completion are read from game state, not model judgement; iteration counts are comparable across methods. The metric aligns with the curriculum objective and iteration count ignores LLM-call heterogeneity.

E.causality.reason: Six-way ablation, plus a store-off arm in zero-shot transfer and a transplant into AutoGPT isolate the curriculum, critic and library. Missing: alternative memory/reflection stores at equal budget, call-matched baselines, tabulated ablation numbers.

E.holdout.reason: A fresh-world, unseen-task test with a store-off arm gives genuine held-out reuse evidence; no leakage/overlap guard, library provenance unspecified, and the exploration headline is measured on the same stream that builds the library.

E.statistics.reason: Three trials per method with SD and success fractions including failures (0/3), but no tests or intervals, and ablation results are curves/percentages without variance.

E.cost.reason: Cost is acknowledged only qualitatively (GPT-4 15x GPT-3.5); no token/dollar accounting for the full system, baselines, or library construction.
